701.title: As for me and my house (Joshua 24:14–15)
701.word: As for me and my house
701.hook: the old leader says: choose this day whom you'll serve
701.howItsDone: Some Christian families hang Joshua 24:15 in their homes, over a door or in the kitchen, as a statement of what their household serves.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the walls of Jericho, and your line was wrestle with hard texts. What did you stay with a minute longer than usual? Day seven hundred one.

Some families hang a line from today's chapter over the front door, or paint it on a kitchen wall: "as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD." On a plaque it looks like a cozy motto. In the story it's the end of a hard speech. Joshua is old. The text says God has given Israel rest. He gathers the tribes at Shechem, with their elders, heads, judges and officers, and tells their whole history back to them: Abraham's father beyond the river, Egypt, the sea, the wilderness, the land under their feet. Then he stops telling the story and asks them to make a decision. Today is that decision.

Here it is, in the King James Bible: "Now therefore fear the LORD, and serve him in sincerity and in truth: and put away the gods which your fathers served on the other side of the flood, and in Egypt; and serve ye the LORD." That word flood isn't Noah's. In the King James it means the river: verse two says Abraham's father Terah lived on the other side of it. Joshua is saying: your ancestors served other gods, back there. Then verse fifteen: "choose you this day whom ye will serve; whether the gods which your fathers served that were on the other side of the flood, or the gods of the Amorites, in whose land ye dwell: but as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD." Notice three things. First, the word serve keeps coming back. Israel came out of the house of bondage, out of serving Pharaoh. The question was never whether they'd serve something. It was whom. Second, the choice is real and specific: the old gods of the family, or the local gods of the neighbors. The pull of the past, and the pull of fitting in. Third, Joshua decides for his own house in the same breath as the question. He doesn't wait for a vote. The people answer: "God forbid that we should forsake the LORD, to serve other gods." And then Joshua says something startling: "Ye cannot serve the LORD: for he is an holy God." He presses them, and they answer again, "Nay; but we will serve the LORD." Only then does he write it in a book and set up a great stone under an oak, a witness that has heard every word. The line that ends up on plaques is, in the story, a choice made on one particular day, out loud, by one household, before anyone else had answered.
screen: then, large: `AS FOR ME AND MY HOUSE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose one thing for your household. Settle, and breathe. Your household might be a family, roommates, a partner, or just you and a cat. Let an ordinary week pass in front of you: meals, screens, mornings, money, the way people speak to each other. What does your home actually serve, day to day? Don't judge it. Just see it. Then choose one small thing your house will do on purpose: a meal without phones, a word of thanks at dinner, a quiet first five minutes of the morning. Choose it now, even if nobody else has agreed yet. If you pray, you can offer that choice to God. The bell holds the time.
As for me and my house. Joshua's answer to his own question: a choice for his household, made today, before anyone else decides.
screen: `AS FOR ME AND MY HOUSE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: choose this day. Today, tell someone in your house the one thing you chose, or write it where you'll see it tonight. Day seven hundred one.

702.title: The cycle (Judges 2:16–19)
702.hook: forget, suffer, cry out, be rescued, forget again: the book of Judges in one loop
702.howItsDone: Some Christians read Judges 2 as the key to the whole book, and some preachers use its cycle to speak about patterns of forgetting God and returning.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Joshua's last speech at Shechem, and your line was choose this day. What did you choose for your house? Day seven hundred two.

Forget. Suffer. Cry out. Be rescued. Forget again. That is the book of Judges in one loop, and the book lays it out itself, near the start, before any of its famous stories begin. Joshua has died, and his whole generation with him. Then the text says it plainly: "there arose another generation after them, which knew not the LORD, nor yet the works which he had done for Israel." The people who carried stones up out of the river are gone. The next generation, it seems, never heard the answer to the question the stones were built to raise. What follows is a loop, and today's word names the people God keeps sending into it.

The word is judge. In English it sounds like a courtroom: a robe, a bench, a gavel. Listen to how the book introduces them, in the King James Bible: "Nevertheless the LORD raised up judges, which delivered them out of the hand of those that spoiled them." Delivered. These judges are rescuers first: leaders raised up in a crisis. Some lead in battle. Some settle disputes. The Hebrew word is shofet. Now the loop. The people turn to other gods. They're handed over to raiders. They groan under it, and here the text says something tender: "it repented the LORD because of their groanings by reason of them that oppressed them and vexed them." God is moved by their groaning. A judge is raised up, and while that judge lives, there's rest. Then verse nineteen: "when the judge was dead, that they returned, and corrupted themselves more than their fathers." More than their fathers. It isn't a circle. It's a spiral, and it's heading down. By the very last verse of the book, the narrator puts it in one line: "In those days there was no king in Israel: every man did that which was right in his own eyes." Readers find two things in this loop at once. One is a warning: the first step is forgetting, and forgetting makes no noise. In chapter two, a generation grows up without the story first, and only then do the other gods follow. The other is mercy. Again and again, when they cry out, someone is sent. What runs short is remembering.

Here's the practice: notice one loop in your life. Settle, and breathe. Loops are often quiet: the same argument, the same late-night scrolling, the same promise on Monday that's gone by Thursday. Let one come to mind. Trace it slowly. Where does it start? What's the forgetting part, the moment you stop paying attention? Where's the groaning? What usually rescues you, for a while? Don't fix it now. Just see the whole loop once, clearly, without beating yourself up. If you pray, you can name it to God, the way Israel groaned. If you don't, simply hold it in view and breathe. The bell holds the time.
Judge. In the book of Judges, a shofet: someone raised up in a crisis to deliver and set things right. Not a robe and a gavel.
Your line: break the cycle. Today, find the forgetting point in your loop, and put one small reminder right there, where it starts. Day seven hundred two.

703.title: Deborah under the palm (Judges 4–5)
703.hook: a prophet and judge who leads an army and sings the victory song
703.howItsDone: Deborah's story is told in Sunday schools and sermons as the story of a prophet and judge of Israel, and churches draw different conclusions from it about women's leadership in church today.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the loop of Judges, and your word was judge: a deliverer, not a gavel. Where did you put your reminder to break the cycle? Day seven hundred three.

Between Ramah and Bethel, in the hill country of Ephraim, stands a palm tree with a name: the palm tree of Deborah. People come up to it with their disputes, and a woman sits beneath it and decides them. The King James gives her three descriptions in one line: "And Deborah, a prophetess, the wife of Lapidoth, she judged Israel at that time." Israel is in the loop again. A Canaanite king, Jabin, has nine hundred chariots of iron, and the text says he has crushed them for twenty years. His general is Sisera. One day, Deborah sends for a man named Barak. Today: what she tells him, and the song she sings when it's over.

Deborah tells Barak that God commands him to gather ten thousand men at Mount Tabor, and God will draw Sisera out to meet him. Barak's answer is honest: "If thou wilt go with me, then I will go: but if thou wilt not go with me, then I will not go." Readers argue over that line. Some hear hesitation. Others hear a man who knows where God's word is coming from and wants the prophet beside him. Deborah says yes, and adds a twist: the honor won't be his, "for the LORD shall sell Sisera into the hand of a woman." On the day itself, she is the one who says go: "Up; for this is the day in which the LORD hath delivered Sisera into thine hand: is not the LORD gone out before thee?" Sisera's army breaks, and Sisera flees on foot to the tent of a woman named Jael, who kills him while he sleeps. So the woman of the prophecy isn't Deborah at all. It's Jael. Then, in chapter five, Deborah and Barak sing. It's a fierce poem. The stars fight from heaven; the river Kishon sweeps the enemy away. And in the middle of it, Deborah names herself. The villages had emptied, life on the roads had stopped, "until that I Deborah arose, that I arose a mother in Israel." A mother in Israel. The chapters never mention children of hers. She's a mother of a people: the one who got them up and moving again. The Bible calls her prophet and judge and gives no explanation for why a woman sits under the palm. She is simply there, and the people come up to her.
screen: `IS NOT THE LORD GONE OUT BEFORE THEE?`
`THE WOMAN IN THE PROPHECY IS JAEL.`
then, large: `I AROSE A MOTHER IN ISRAEL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor a woman leader you know. Settle, and breathe. Let one woman come to mind who got people up and moving: a grandmother who held a family together, a teacher, a manager, a nurse, a coach, the neighbor who organizes everyone. Someone people came to, the way they came up to the palm. See her face. What did she do that nobody thanked her for? Let your gratitude settle on that one specific thing. If you pray, you can give thanks for her by name. If you don't, simply hold her in mind and breathe. The bell holds the time.
Deborah under the palm. A prophet and judge whom Israel came up to for judgment; she called the battle, and she sang the song.
Your line: a mother in israel. Today, tell the woman you thought of, in a message or out loud, one specific thing she did that mattered. Day seven hundred three.

704.title: Gideon in the winepress (Judges 6:11–16)
704.hook: hiding while threshing wheat, the least of his family is called mighty man of valor
704.howItsDone: Some Christians turn to Gideon's call when they feel too small for a task, and some preachers use the greeting 'mighty man of valour' to speak about God naming people for what they can become.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Deborah under the palm, and your line was a mother in israel. Did you tell her the thing she did? Day seven hundred four.

A man is threshing wheat in a winepress. That's an odd place for it. A winepress is a pit for treading grapes, and he's down inside it beating out grain where nobody passing by can see. The text gives the reason: "to hide it from the Midianites." Raiders have been sweeping in when the crops come up and stripping the land, and Israel has taken to dens and caves in the mountains. His name is Gideon. While he's crouched in that pit, a stranger, the angel of the LORD, sits down under an oak nearby and greets him with words that, in that moment, sound almost absurd.

In the King James Bible: "The LORD is with thee, thou mighty man of valour." Mighty man of valor. To a man hiding in a hole. Gideon doesn't take the compliment. He argues, and his first argument is about God, not himself: "Oh my Lord, if the LORD be with us, why then is all this befallen us?" And where, he asks, are all the miracles our fathers told us about? It's a raw question, and the text lets it stand. What he gets back isn't an explanation. It's a job: "Go in this thy might, and thou shalt save Israel from the hand of the Midianites: have not I sent thee?" In this thy might. What might? So Gideon tries a second argument, this time about himself: "Oh my Lord, wherewith shall I save Israel? behold, my family is poor in Manasseh, and I am the least in my father's house." A poor family in his tribe, and the least in his own house. He's telling the truth as he sees it. And the reply doesn't argue with that. It doesn't say you're stronger than you think. It says: "Surely I will be with thee." Here's the turn. The name comes first. Gideon is called mighty man of valor before he has done one brave thing. Some readers hear God seeing what Gideon will become. Others hear a name he can grow into only because God goes with him. Either way, the word arrives before the evidence. And Gideon still isn't convinced. He asks for a sign, and before long he'll ask for more: a fleece left out overnight, wet and then dry. The Bible doesn't hide his doubting. It keeps him in the story anyway.
screen: `MIGHTY MAN OF VALOR, IN A HOLE.`
`WHY THEN IS ALL THIS BEFALLEN US?`
`I AM THE LEAST IN MY FATHER'S HOUSE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: accept a compliment you don't feel. Settle, and breathe. Bring back something kind someone once said about you that you waved away: you're a good friend, you're brave, you're good at this. Hear it again, in their voice. Notice what rises up to argue with it, the way Gideon argued: my family is poor, I am the least. Don't argue back. Don't force yourself to agree, either. Just let the words stay in the room with you while you breathe. If you pray, you can let God hear the argument too, as Gideon did. If you don't, simply let the kind words stay. The bell holds the time.
Gideon in the winepress. A man hiding his grain in a pit, called mighty man of valor before he had done anything brave.
Your line: you, mighty? Today, when someone says something kind about you, say thank you, and stop there. No arguing. Day seven hundred four.

705.title: Three hundred (Judges 7)
705.hook: God shrinks Gideon's army so no one will boast
705.howItsDone: Some Christians tell the story of Gideon's three hundred to speak about God's strength showing up in human weakness, and some pair it with Paul's words in Second Corinthians that strength is made perfect in weakness.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gideon in the winepress, and your line was you, mighty? Did you take a kind word without arguing? Day seven hundred five.

Gideon finally has an army, and God's complaint is not that it's too small. In the King James Bible: "The people that are with thee are too many for me to give the Midianites into their hands, lest Israel vaunt themselves against me, saying, Mine own hand hath saved me." Too many. Gideon's men are camped by a spring, and below them in the valley lies the camp of Midian and its allies, "like grasshoppers for multitude," the text says, with camels past counting. Any sensible general would be sending messengers for more troops. Gideon is told to send people home. Today's title is the number he's left with.

First cut: whoever is fearful and afraid may go home. The text says twenty-two thousand leave and ten thousand stay. Still too many, God says. Second cut: take them down to the water to drink. Some get down on their knees to drink. Some lap, the text says, putting their hand to their mouth. Three hundred lap. Those are the ones God keeps: "By the three hundred men that lapped will I save you." The text never explains why the lappers were chosen. Some preachers say they were the alert ones, keeping their eyes up. Others say the test was arbitrary on purpose, and God simply took the smaller group. Judges gives no reason at all. It isn't a test of who's best. The reason it does give is back in verse two: so that Israel can't say, mine own hand hath saved me. Then comes the plan, and it's strange. Each of the three hundred gets a trumpet and an empty pitcher with a lamp hidden inside. In the middle of the night they spread out around the camp, blow the trumpets, smash the pitchers so the lights blaze out, and cry: "The sword of the LORD, and of Gideon." And then: "they stood every man in his place round about the camp." They don't charge. They hold up their lights and stand still. The camp panics and turns on itself. Notice the order of that cry: the sword of the LORD first, Gideon second. The whole chapter is built so that, afterward, nobody can tell it as a story about their own strength. Less isn't a punishment here. Less is how they find out who did the saving.
screen: `THE TEXT NEVER SAYS WHY THE LAPPERS.`
then, large: `THE SWORD OF THE LORD, AND OF GIDEON.`
`THEY STOOD EVERY MAN IN HIS PLACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do something with less than you'd like. Settle, and breathe. Is there one thing on your plate today you feel under-equipped for: not enough time, not enough money, not enough help, not enough sleep? Name it. Then, instead of listing everything you lack, count what you actually have, the way Gideon counted at the water. Three hundred is a real number. So is one free hour, or two friends, or forty dollars. Ask what you could do with exactly that. If you pray, you can bring the gap to God. If you don't, simply breathe, and let the small number be enough for now. The bell holds the time.
Three hundred. The men who lapped the water: the army God made smaller, so no one could say, my own hand saved me.
Your line: less is enough. Today, start the thing you named with what you have, and don't wait for more. Day seven hundred five.

706.title: Samson's last prayer (Judges 16:23–30)
706.hook: blind and shackled, the strong man prays one more time
706.howItsDone: Christians read Samson's story in more than one way, as a warning about strength without wisdom and as a sign that a prayer from the lowest place is still heard, and some point out that Hebrews 11:32 still lists his name.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gideon's three hundred, and your line was less is enough. What did you start with only what you had? Day seven hundred six.

"Call for Samson, that he may make us sport." That's a crowd at a feast. The lords of the Philistines have gathered at the temple of their god Dagon to celebrate, and they say their god has delivered their enemy into their hand. The enemy is Samson, the strong man of Israel: betrayed by Delilah, his hair shaved, his eyes put out, bound with fetters of brass and set to grinding at the mill in the prison house. Now they bring him out to amuse them. A boy leads him by the hand. The text says about three thousand men and women are on the roof alone, watching. And there's one small line, a few verses back, that the reader knows and the crowd doesn't.
screen: `A BOY LEADS HIM BY THE HAND.`

segments.voice: Here's the line, verse twenty-two: "Howbeit the hair of his head began to grow again after he was shaven." Samson asks the boy to let him feel the pillars the house stands on. Then he prays. In the King James Bible: "O Lord GOD, remember me, I pray thee, and strengthen me, I pray thee, only this once, O God, that I may be at once avenged of the Philistines for my two eyes." It's worth hearing honestly. This is not a gentle prayer. Samson asks for revenge, for his eyes. Some readers sum up his whole story that way: strong, impulsive, careless with the vow over his life. And yet the text keeps this prayer, and the prayer is answered. Look at the first words, though, before the anger: remember me. He doesn't open with his rights or his record. He asks to be remembered. And only this once. He seems to know he has no credit left. Then: "Let me die with the Philistines." He bows himself with all his might, the pillars give way, and the house falls on the lords and on the people. The chapter closes with a grim tally: those he killed at his death were more than those he killed in his life. Readers don't agree on how to hear this ending. Some hear a sacrifice. Some hear a tragedy, a man whose strength was never matched by wisdom. Centuries later, Hebrews chapter eleven reaches him in a hurry. The writer runs out of room and starts listing names: "the time would fail me to tell of Gedeon, and of Barak, and of Samson." No verdict, no story, just the name, set beside the man from the winepress. Some readers say that's enough. At the very end, blind, shackled and mocked, he still knew whom to call.

Here's the practice: speak from your weakest place. Settle, and breathe. Let your attention go to a place where you're not strong right now: something you've lost, a mistake you keep paying for, a part of your life that feels shackled. Don't dress it up. Samson didn't. If you pray, you can borrow the first words of his prayer, only those: remember me. Say them, and stop. If you don't pray, simply hold that weak place gently, the way you'd hold someone else's, and breathe. Nothing needs fixing in two minutes. The bell holds the time.
Samson's last prayer. Blind and shackled in the temple of Dagon, the strong man asks: remember me, and strengthen me, only this once.
Your line: remember me, just this once. Today, ask for help with the weak thing you named, from God or from a person, in one plain sentence. Day seven hundred six.

707.title: Whither thou goest (Ruth 1)
707.hook: a widowed Moabite refuses to leave her mother-in-law: your people shall be my people
707.howItsDone: Christians read Ruth's vow as a picture of faithful love that crosses family, nation and grief, a love that holds on when the other person has stopped hoping.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Samson's last prayer, and your line was remember me, just this once. Who did you ask for help, and how plain was the sentence? Day seven hundred seven.

Three widows on a road out of Moab. The book of Ruth opens "in the days when the judges ruled," the same troubled years we've just walked through, and it opens small. A famine in Bethlehem. A man named Elimelech takes his wife Naomi and their two sons to Moab to find food. He dies there. The sons marry Moabite women, Orpah and Ruth. About ten years go by, and both sons die too. Now Naomi hears that the LORD has given his people bread again, and she starts for home with her two daughters-in-law. Somewhere on that road she stops and turns around. Go back, she tells them. Each of you, go back to your mother's house. I have nothing left to give you.
screen: `GO BACK, EACH TO YOUR MOTHER'S HOUSE.`

segments.voice: They weep. Then the two women choose differently, and the text puts it in one short verse: "Orpah kissed her mother in law; but Ruth clave unto her." Notice that Orpah isn't blamed. She does what Naomi asked, and kisses her goodbye. The story blames neither woman. It simply stays with the harder choice. Clave is the old past tense of cleave, to hold fast. The King James uses the same word in Genesis, where a man shall leave his father and mother "and shall cleave unto his wife." Here it's a daughter-in-law holding on to a mother-in-law, a Moabite to an Israelite, a young widow to an old one with nothing to offer. Naomi tries once more, and Ruth answers with the lines this day is named for: "Intreat me not to leave thee, or to return from following after thee: for whither thou goest, I will go; and where thou lodgest, I will lodge: thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God." Listen to how it climbs. The road. The bed. The people. God. Then she keeps going, all the way down: where you die, I'll die, and there I'll be buried. She isn't promising a trip. She's promising a whole life, and a grave in a foreign country. The text says that when Naomi saw she was steadfastly minded, she stopped arguing. Then a detail that's easy to miss. When the two of them reach Bethlehem and the town comes out to look, Naomi says, "Call me not Naomi, call me Mara: for the Almighty hath dealt very bitterly with me." And: "I went out full, and the LORD hath brought me home again empty." Empty. Ruth is standing right beside her. Some readers hear a grief so deep it doesn't count her. Ruth stays anyway. The chapter ends at the start of barley harvest, which matters tomorrow.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stay with someone who's lost much. Settle, and breathe. Let one person come to mind who is carrying a loss right now: a death, a divorce, a job, their health. Maybe they're bitter. Maybe they've stopped noticing who's still around. Don't wait for them to thank you. Nobody thanks Ruth here. Just hold them in mind for these two minutes, and decide one way you'll stay close this week. A call. A meal. Sitting with them. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. The bell holds the time.

Whither thou goest. Ruth's vow on the road out of Moab, spoken to her widowed mother-in-law: whither thou goest, I will go. It closes a week that ran from Joshua's choose this day, through the judges, to one widow on a road.
Your line: where you go, I go. Today, show up for the person you named, even in a small way, without needing them to notice. Day seven hundred seven.

original.note: Hebrew: clave, held fast. Ruth 1:14 says Ruth clave unto Naomi.
